documents.title: Guidance on the Use of Generative AI
documents.summary: Northwestern IT guidance on generative AI that defines the term, warns about privacy and bias, and tells users not to enter institutional data into unvalidated tools. It sends teaching and learning questions to the Provost's committee and sets no classroom stance.
documents.stance_why: The page gives data and tool guidance and says teaching use "is governed by the Provost's Committee on Generative AI" and found on the Provost site, so it sets no stance on student AI use and hands it to others.

units.why: The sentence frames why the guidance exists: it says understanding what to look for in adopting tools is "key to ensuring the intended use is met while protecting University data", an institution-level purpose statement, so P56 (framework/preamble) with informs and general.
units.anchor: key to ensuring the intended use is met while protecting University data

units.why: Defines generative AI as "artificial intelligence that creates new content based on patterns from the data sets used to train it", which sets what the guidance covers, so P61 (definitions) and informs.
units.anchor: Generative AI is a general term for artificial intelligence that creates new content

units.why: States that generative AI "is also now embedded in many commercial products" such as Otter AI and Zoom IQ, widening the scope to AI inside other tools. It is a scope fact, closest to P61; P07 covers rules about built-in AI but this sets no rule.
units.anchor: Generative AI is also now embedded in many commercial products
units.policy: Generative AI is embedded in many commercial products that can be integrated with other tools.
units.fit_note: Also notes AI embedded in other products (like P07) but states no rule about it.

units.why: Warns that "the data you share as part of your queries in generative AI tools will be accessible by others" because tools store user input, a privacy fact, so P50 with informs.
units.anchor: queries in generative AI tools will be accessible by others

units.why: Directive that faculty, staff, students and affiliates "should not enter institutional data into any generative AI tools that have not been validated by the University". It limits data input to vetted tools, so P50 (prefer vetted tools), should-not, restrict.
units.anchor: should not enter institutional data into any generative AI tools that have not been validated

units.why: Points users to the Tools and Use Guidance page "to find the right AI tool and review what types of data are allowed" under the data classification levels; this steers users to approved tools per data level, so P50.
units.anchor: to find the right AI tool and review what types of data are allowed

units.why: Says teaching and learning use of generative AI "is governed by the Provost's Committee on Generative AI, in tandem with Northwestern IT". It assigns governance of academic use to a body and sets no stance, so P56 and informs.
units.anchor: Use of generative AI for teaching and learning purposes is governed by the Provost
units.fit_note: Defers teaching-and-learning rules to the Provost's committee rather than stating them.

units.why: Routes research-related AI questions to Research Computing and Data Services. It is a research-use channel; P62 (AI in research) is nearest but it states no research rule.
units.anchor: Questions about AI usage pertaining to research applications can be directed to
units.fit_note: Only names who to ask about research AI use; sets no rule on research.

units.why: Routes questions on security, privacy, Level 2 or above data and "evaluation of new third-party AI products" to the Information Security Office, a review route for AI vendor tools, so P65 as nearest.
units.anchor: evaluation of new third-party AI products can be directed to
units.fit_note: Names where to send third-party AI product evaluations; does not itself describe the contract review or data-sharing limits in P65.

units.why: States that generative AI models "will invariably tend to suppress less common or marginalized information", a bias concern, so P53 and informs.
units.anchor: will invariably tend to suppress less common or marginalized information
units.policy: Generative AI models tend to suppress less common or marginalized information.

units.why: States that tools "can hallucinate or make up random data that is not true", a fact that output can be wrong, so P31 with informs.
units.anchor: these tools can “hallucinate” or make up random data that is not true

units.why: Under the heading "Revalidation of output is required", it says tools "should be periodically re-validated to ensure appropriate responses" where accuracy matters. This is a verify-output duty, so P31 with should.
units.anchor: these tools should be periodically re-validated to ensure appropriate responses
units.fit_note: Asks for periodic re-validation of tools over time, not only checking each output.

units.why: Requires that "necessary approvals for use of original works and intellectual property are obtained prior to input into generative AI tools", naming student works and copyrighted material. It limits what may be put into AI tools, so P49; P52 covers ownership of outputs, which this does not.
units.anchor: Ensure necessary approvals for use of original works and intellectual property are obtained
units.fit_note: Covers approvals for original works, research results and copyrighted material, wider than course materials in P49.

units.why: States "Users have the right to know when they are using generative AI tools", a transparency principle about users being told about AI, which no type covers; it is neither student disclosure (P24) nor instructor disclosure (P47).
units.anchor: Users have the right to know when they are using generative AI tools
units.uncovered_note: Users have a right to know when they are interacting with generative AI (informed consent), as a general principle.

documents.title: Generative AI Advisory Committee
documents.summary: The Provost's AI and Education Advisory Committee page lists its charge, responsibilities and members. It describes a decentralized structure where schools and departments write local guidance.
documents.stance_why: The page describes a committee charge and says "schools and departments" craft "context-specific guidance" and instructors should "consult with their school and department/program", so no stance is set and the decision is delegated.

units.why: Describes the committee as "a strategic body to guide Northwestern's response to the emergence of artificial intelligence" in teaching and learning, an institution-level charge, so P56.
units.anchor: a strategic body to guide Northwestern
units.frag_end: as AI and related technologies advance.

units.why: Charges the committee with advising the Provost on "academic integrity and instructional policy and practices", which sets who maintains AI teaching policy, so P56 and informs.
units.anchor: advising the Provost on pedagogical issues and resource development related to AI
units.frag_end: as AI and related technologies advance.

units.why: Lists "Review policies developed by the Office of the Provost and related units" among responsibilities, a standing review role; closest is P54 although no review cycle is given.
units.anchor: Review policies developed by the Office of the Provost and related units
units.fit_note: Gives a standing policy-review role but states no schedule or promise to revise.

units.why: Responsibility to "Advance instructor engagement through workshops, seminars and conferences", which is faculty support for learning about AI, so P63.
units.anchor: Advance instructor engagement through workshops, seminars and conferences

units.why: Responsibility to "Promote student literacy and responsible use of AI for learning", an institutional commitment to student AI literacy, so P70.
units.anchor: Promote student literacy and responsible use of AI for learning

units.why: Charge to "Reimagine the future of learning and teaching with AI by advancing leading-edge pedagogical practices". It welcomes AI in pedagogy as a goal; no type covers an institution aiming to advance AI-based teaching, so UNCOVERED.
units.anchor: Reimagine the future of learning and teaching with AI
units.uncovered_note: The committee aims to advance leading-edge AI-based pedagogical practices and classroom environments.

units.why: Responsibility to "Identify and reduce barriers to instructor adoption of AI by streamlining access to tools, resources and support". It is support for instructors using AI, so P63.
units.anchor: Identify and reduce barriers to instructor adoption of AI
units.fit_note: Also aims to streamline access to AI tools for instructors.

units.why: Says units such as Teaching and Learning Technologies, the Libraries and the Searle Center "offer different tools, resources and programs" for integrating AI in teaching, which is instructional support, so P63.
units.anchor: Each unit offers different tools, resources and programs tailored to support the thoughtful integration

units.why: States that "This decentralized structure allows schools and departments to craft context-specific guidance", so rules are set locally and not by one university rule, which is P04.
units.anchor: This decentralized structure allows schools and departments to craft context-specific guidance

units.why: "We encourage instructors to consult with their school and department/program for local policies on the use of AI in teaching" sends instructors to local rules rather than setting one, so P04 with should.
units.anchor: We encourage instructors to consult with their school and department/program for local policies
units.fit_note: Tells instructors to look up local policies; it does not itself let instructors decide.

documents.unit: Weinberg College of Arts and Sciences
documents.title: Academic Integrity and Artificial Intelligence: Principles and Guidelines
documents.summary: Weinberg College principles say AI-generated work presented as one's own breaches academic integrity. AI may be used in coursework only as instructors permit, with disclosure and asking first when unsure.
documents.stance_why: The document says "artificial intelligence may be used for coursework only as specifically permitted by instructors", so AI is banned unless permitted, which is restrict.

units.why: Says students "may not present the work of others, including work generated by artificial intelligence or LLMs, as if it were their own", banning AI-generated work submitted as own, so P19, must-not, prohibit.
units.anchor: may not present the work of others, including work generated by artificial intelligence or LLMs
units.frag_end: as if it were their own.

units.why: Says "we want students to produce academic work in good faith", with sources "directly consulted"; students must stand behind genuine work, so P29 with should.
units.anchor: we want students to produce academic work in good faith
units.frag_end: directly consulted as part of the process.
units.fit_note: Good faith includes citing only sources the student has directly consulted.

units.why: States that "fragments or summaries of scholarship generated by online tools must not replace one's own research and analysis". It keeps the student as the thinker, so P32 rather than P19, because the concern is replacing own analysis.
units.anchor: must not replace one’s own research and analysis

units.why: Says coursework "always aims to create space for both the process and product of learning" and "the goal is far more than the generation of a final product", a reason to do the work oneself, so P41.
units.anchor: it always aims to create space for both the process and product of learning

units.why: Says LLMs "cannot always be trusted to deliver accurate information, exhibit true judgment, or be held accountable", so output is unreliable, P31 and informs.
units.anchor: they cannot always be trusted to deliver accurate information

units.why: States AI "can supplement research and learning, but it should not replace the effort that leads to distinctly human discernment", keeping thinking with the student, so P32 and should-not.
units.anchor: it should not replace the effort that leads to distinctly human discernment

units.why: Sets the college default: AI "may be used for coursework only as specifically permitted by instructors", so it is banned unless permitted, which is P01 (default ban); the permission step also makes it instructor-set, so I chose P01 as the default rule.
units.anchor: artificial intelligence may be used for coursework only as specifically permitted by instructors
units.fit_note: Default ban is lifted only by explicit instructor permission, also a delegation (P04).

units.why: Says instructors who allow AI "should clearly describe in their course policies how students may and may not use AI", which asks for a stated AI policy, so P09 with should.
units.anchor: should clearly describe in their course policies how students may and may not use AI
units.frag_start: Instructors who allow students to use AI
units.frag_end: use AI to support or augment their own work
units.fit_note: Applies only to instructors who allow AI, not to every syllabus.

units.why: Adds "students should adhere to these policies", making instructor course policies binding, which fits P04 (instructor sets the rule) only partly.
units.anchor: students should adhere to these policies
units.frag_start: Instructors who allow students to use AI
units.frag_end: students should adhere to these policies.
units.fit_note: States the student duty to follow the instructor policy rather than who sets it.

units.why: Says "students should be prepared to say how AI was used or consulted" in courses allowing AI, a disclosure expectation, so P24 with should.
units.anchor: students should be prepared to say how AI was used or consulted
units.fit_note: Asks students to be ready to say how AI was used, not necessarily to file a statement.

units.why: Says "it will be important for instructors to be clear about whether AI may be used to support coursework" because AI is embedded in tools; this asks for stated expectations, so P09 with should.
units.anchor: it will be important for instructors to be clear about whether AI may be used
units.frag_start: Given the various ways AI is embedded

units.why: Gives as an example of appropriate use: "it may be appropriate to use AI to create flash cards or other study tools", a study aid use, so P14, may, permit.
units.anchor: it may be appropriate to use AI to create flash cards or other study tools
units.frag_start: For example, it may be appropriate

units.why: Gives as possibly unacceptable "have AI summarize texts in lieu of reading them". The concern is replacing the student's own reading and thinking, so P32 rather than P19, and should-not because the text says "may not be acceptable".
units.anchor: have AI summarize texts in lieu of reading them
units.frag_start: But it may not be acceptable

units.why: Gives as possibly unacceptable "solve problem sets before attempting them"; it protects the student's own first attempt, so P32 and should-not.
units.anchor: solve problem sets before attempting them
units.frag_start: But it may not be acceptable
units.fit_note: Ties the limit to order: AI solving before the student attempts, not AI use as such.

units.why: Gives as possibly unacceptable having AI "edit prose for them", a limit on AI for writing, so P21 (no AI to proofread or check graded work); P18 treats prose separately but this reads as a ban, so P21.
units.anchor: edit prose for them
units.frag_start: But it may not be acceptable
units.fit_note: Concerns editing prose, which P21 lists as proofreading.

units.why: Says students unsure whether a use is appropriate "should always ask the instructor in advance", exactly P10.
units.anchor: they should always ask the instructor in advance
units.frag_start: If students aren’t sure whether a particular

notes: Provost's Generative AI Policy for Teaching and Coursework (Evanston) not collected; no computing-unit policy. Coded three included documents only. Topic codes taken from codes used in existing v2/inst files because AGENT_BRIEF.md was not found.
